title: Scivias I.6: The Choirs of Angels

image.credit: Collection not stated on source page; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: A medieval drawing in ink and gold leaf that illustrates a religious vision of groups of angels, called choirs. The figures and gold are arranged in an ordered, flat, symbolic way rather than a realistic scene.

source.museum: Collection not stated on source page
source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: A medieval drawing in ink and gold leaf dated 1150 on the art site and attributed to Hildegard von Bingen. The page says it illustrates one of the 26 religious visions she collected in the Scivias, which describe the creation and structure of the universe and the story of salvation. It is tagged Angels and Catholicism. The page does not state which collection holds it.

descriptions.k: This very old picture shows groups of angels. It was made with ink and shiny gold. Look for the gold. Look for the groups of figures. What do you see?
descriptions.g12: This picture is about 900 years old. Hildegard von Bingen made it to show groups of angels called choirs. It was made with ink and shiny gold leaf. Look at how the figures are arranged. What do you see? Which part looks the most special?
descriptions.g35: This drawing, Scivias I.6: The Choirs of Angels, was made around 1150 with ink and gold leaf. It illustrates one of 26 religious visions that Hildegard von Bingen wrote down. The art site tags it with angels and Catholicism. Look at how the figures are arranged and where the gold appears. What do you think the artist wanted viewers to notice?
descriptions.g68: Scivias I.6: The Choirs of Angels (about 1150) is an ink and gold leaf drawing that illustrates one of the 26 visions Hildegard von Bingen collected in her Scivias. The visions describe the creation and structure of the universe and the story of salvation. This image shows angels arranged in groups. How does the picture organize its figures, and what does the gold add to the page?
descriptions.g910: Scivias I.6: The Choirs of Angels (about 1150) is a medieval drawing in ink and gold leaf that accompanies one of Hildegard von Bingen's 26 visions, which describe the structure of the universe and the story of salvation. The image presents angels in organized groups, not in a realistic space. How do arrangement, line and gold work together to express religious ideas, and what makes medieval images different from modern ones?
descriptions.g1112: Scivias I.6: The Choirs of Angels (about 1150) is an ink and gold leaf illustration linked to Hildegard von Bingen's Scivias, a collection of 26 visions about creation, the universe and salvation. Its angels are ordered into groups within a flat, symbolic space rather than a naturalistic one. How does the image translate a visionary text into visual structure, and what does the use of gold leaf contribute to its meaning and its status as a crafted object?

teacherNote.context: A medieval ink and gold leaf drawing, dated 1150 on the art site, linked to Hildegard von Bingen's Scivias. It illustrates her vision of the choirs, or groups, of angels. Treat it as devotional art made for a religious community.
directions: Explain that this was a handmade book illustration, and invite students to discuss how the care taken with materials shows the value placed on the book.
Have students draw a group, such as a team or choir, in ordered rows or circles to show relationships, adding a metallic marker or crayon for emphasis.
Remind students to describe religious art respectfully, focusing on what the artist made and how, and ask older students to compare how different cultures show sacred figures.
